source_metadata.title: TEPA: Revoking Stale Memories for Conflict-Robust Language Agents
source_metadata.input_file: TEPA Revoking Stale Memories for Conflict-Robust Language Agents - 2608.07429v1.pdf

atoms.canonical_statement: The study evaluates whether stale active long-term memories can make language-agent performance worse than no memory and whether conflict-keyed revocation prevents that failure.
Memory pollution is defined as degradation caused by active memories that have been superseded by newer conflicting evidence.

TEPA represents observations as keyed precedents with explicit lifecycle validity state and revokes an active precedent when fresh same-key evidence contradicts it, while retaining the revoked history for audit.
Stale-conflict consolidation asks the agent to answer using the current value for each key when later evidence supersedes an earlier incompatible value under the same key.
Two evidence items are treated as conflicting when they share a conflict key but assert incompatible values.
Revocable memory separates active precedents eligible for retrieval from a revoked archive excluded from ordinary retrieval.
The memory pollution index is the phase-wise relative gap between no-memory success and method success, divided by no-memory success.
A positive memory pollution index means the memory method performs worse than no memory in that phase.
A TEPA precedent stores a conflict key, asserted value or action pattern, support count, conflict count, lifecycle state, and creation time; only Active precedents are retrievable.
In the drift benchmarks, retrieval returns active precedents matching the current task key and orders them by recency within that key.
In MemoryAgentBench, all compared methods use the same lexical top-k answer context after the memory-state update.
TEPA estimates precedent validity with a Beta-Bernoulli posterior mean q(p)=(s+alpha)/(s+f+alpha+beta), using alpha=beta=1 in all experiments.
Same-value evidence increments an active precedent support count, while incompatible same-key evidence increments its conflict count.
An active precedent is revoked when its posterior mean falls below 0.3 after at least 5 observations or when, after at least 3 recent same-key outcomes, recent success falls below 0.34.
TEPA uses Hypothesis for candidates before promotion, Active for retrievable precedents, and Revoked for precedents contradicted by fresher same-key evidence.
Fresh evidence can later promote a new precedent under the same key after an older precedent has been revoked.
TEPA-Full adds trial-by-execution before promotion, with a default budget of one support check, one counterfactual check, and one contamination check.
A TEPA-Full candidate is promoted after at least 60% of validation trials are positive and at least one support trial succeeds.
TEPA revocation is local to active precedents sharing the conflicting key, preserving unrelated keys for retrieval.

Under the paper's single-key risk view, stale exposure followed with probability xi*eta can outweigh the benefit of useful current memory; when xi*eta exceeds that benefit, append-only memory becomes worse than no memory.

The evaluation uses controlled hidden-regime drift, real file-backed executable drift, a preference-update stream, and MemoryAgentBench SH-6k, with MH-6k and long-context settings used as boundary tests.
Mechanism baselines include no memory, append-only memory, temporal recency, semantic retrieval, sliding window, reactive forgetting, last-write-wins, conflict-aware recency, and oracle reset.

Primary metrics are phase-wise success rate for drift and preference benchmarks and substring exact match for MemoryAgentBench; inference uses bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, paired permutation tests, Holm-Bonferroni correction, and paired effect sizes where applicable.
The paired design compares methods on matched task or query indices to control variance from intrinsic task difficulty.
Controlled, executable, and preference-update benchmarks use deterministic executors to isolate memory behavior from language-model sampling variance.
MemoryAgentBench uses a fixed DeepSeek-v4-Flash answer backend under the same prompt and scoring pipeline for all methods.
The default TEPA configuration uses proposal threshold 3, revocation threshold 0.3, promotion threshold 0.6, and trial budget 3 for TEPA-Full.

Controlled and executable drift use conflict keys composed of task type, domain, and input type; preference updates use preference slot plus profile context; MemoryAgentBench SH-6k keys are parsed from fact subject and relation template.
Deployable methods do not receive hidden phase labels, future phase boundaries, or current hidden regimes; oracle reset alone receives privileged phase information as a diagnostic upper bound.
Each controlled, executable, and preference benchmark uses 50 seeds and 160 tasks per seed, while MemoryAgentBench SH-6k uses three query-order seeds and 300 queries.
During controlled full reversal, append-only, last-write-wins, and conflict-aware recency each achieved 0.210 success, below no memory at 0.309, while TEPA achieved 0.950.

atoms.canonical_statement: TEPA assumes useful conflict keys can be extracted from evidence; this is natural for structured preference slots, entity attributes, and tool-regime records but harder for open-ended memories with implicit conflict relations.

atoms.canonical_statement: Under the key-current model, excluding stale same-key evidence weakly dominates retrieving both stale and current evidence in expected 0-1 loss when the current value remains available; the dominance is strict if stale evidence is sometimes followed.

If append-only retrieval exposes stale evidence with probability q and the downstream decision follows it with probability eta, append-only excess risk over revocable memory is at least q*eta under 0-1 loss, or at least q*eta*Delta when stale following adds loss Delta.

Within a stationary segment, the Beta-Bernoulli posterior mean converges to the precedent support probability; if that probability is below the revocation threshold, revocation eventually occurs almost surely, while false-revocation probability above the threshold decays exponentially after sufficient observations.
The theoretical propositions are restricted to stale single-key conflict revocation and do not provide guarantees for retrieval-chain construction, compositional answering, or long-context selection.
The authors conclude that persistent agent memory should track validity alongside relevance because a memory can remain relevant and recent after its value has been superseded.
The authors conclude that revocation should remove contradicted same-key evidence from ordinary retrieval while preserving revoked precedents for audit, diagnosis, and possible later re-promotion.
The paper explicitly limits its positive claim to conflict-keyed revocation for stale evidence rather than general autonomous-agent memory performance.
The authors identify multi-hop retrieval-chain construction and very-long-context selection as the next architectural challenges beyond fact-level validity tracking.

extraction_limitations: No funding, conflict-of-interest, or data-availability statement was identified in the provided 14-page preprint, so none was invented as an atom.

Quantitative benchmark atoms normalize AI evaluation streams into the current LiteratureAtom population/exposure/outcome schema; these descriptors represent benchmark methods and query/task sets, not human study populations or clinical interventions.
The extraction preserves the paper's own benchmark claims and theoretical scope; it does not externally verify benchmark code, DeepSeek-v4-Flash behavior, referenced prior work, or reproducibility.
Appendix references and bibliography entries were treated as provenance/background infrastructure rather than atom targets unless they contained a direct claim about the present study.
